items.question: Which of the following correctly describes a structural distinction between HTTP GET and POST requests?
options: GET transfers data within the request body, whereas POST appends parameters to the URL.
GET requests cannot be bookmarked by browsers, whereas POST requests are stored in browser history.
GET sends parameters as part of the URL query string, whereas POST transfers parameters inside the request body.
GET is an unsafe method intended to modify server state, whereas POST is strictly read-only.

items.question: A web application form requires users to enter a new password. Why should the web developer configure the form to use POST instead of GET?
options: POST places sensitive form data inside the request body rather than displaying it in the browser URL bar.
GET requests are restricted from sending text strings to web servers.
GET automatically encrypts parameters, whereas POST sends plain text without TLS.
POST is a safe method that guarantees no state changes occur on the backend server.

4xx (Client Error)
2xx (Successful)

items.question: A client sends an HTTP request containing malformed JSON syntax in its request payload. How should the server categorize its response status code?
options: 5xx class because any execution failure must be classified as a server error.
4xx class because the request contains bad syntax or a client-side error.
2xx class because the network packet was successfully delivered.
1xx class to request informational header updates from the client.

items.question: A client receives an unrecognized HTTP status code of 471 from a server. According to the HTTP specification, how must the client handle this response?
options: Treat the response as equivalent to status code 400 (Bad Request).
Crash the application because the status code is unregistered.
Ignore the status code and assume the request succeeded with 200 OK.
Treat the response as equivalent to status code 500 (Internal Server Error).

confusions.quote: Understanding these mechanisms is essential for developing web applications and designing REST APIs [S7, S11].
confusions.why: It mentions REST APIs out of nowhere without explaining what a REST API is, and I have no idea what that means.

confusions.quote: Misconception 1: GET requests can never alter server state, and POST requests are inherently encrypted.
confusions.why: I get confused because it mentions encryption here, but then it says POST is actually not encrypted in plain text, which mixes up my memory about secure passwords.

confusions.quote: both GET and POST transmit data in plain text unless encrypted with TLS/HTTPS
confusions.why: Wait, I always thought POST hid things safely, so finding out it is still in plain text makes me confused about when to actually use it.

confusions.quote: both GET and POST transmit data in plain text unless encrypted with TLS/HTTPS
confusions.why: The lesson introduces TLS/HTTPS here without previously defining it or explaining how it integrates with HTTP, which feels like a sudden jump in networking concepts.

alignment.note: Both methods are thoroughly explained, practised through selection exercises, and assessed in the quiz.

alignment.objective_part: Distinguish between 2xx, 4xx, and 5xx response status categories
alignment.note: Status code categories are taught, classified in practice steps, and tested across multiple quiz questions.

rubric.justification: Every part of the learning objective is explicitly taught, practised, and tested in the quiz.
The concepts are well explained, though minor confusion around TLS/HTTPS and encryption arises in the misconceptions section.
The lesson flows logically from hooks and concepts to Python code examples, misconceptions, practice, and a recap.
The Python urllib examples effectively demonstrate how GET and POST requests are constructed and return status codes.
Section 5 provides concrete scenarios for learners to select methods and classify status code outcomes.
The quiz questions directly align with the objective parts and show complete post-instruction mastery among simulated students.
The computed reading time and planned duration are well balanced, though some sections are dense for their allocated time.
The lesson includes good hooks, real-world Python code, and interactive practice exercises to keep learners engaged.

issues.description: The introduction of TLS/HTTPS creates confusion about plain text transmission versus form parameter safety.
issues.evidence: both GET and POST transmit data in plain text unless encrypted with TLS/HTTPS
issues.suggestion: Add a brief explanatory sentence defining TLS/HTTPS as the transport layer security protocol that encrypts HTTP traffic between the browser and server.
